title: What philosophy is, and logic basics
note: An argument offers premises as reasons for a conclusion. A deductive argument is valid when true premises would guarantee a true conclusion; it is sound when it is valid and its premises really are true. An inductive argument only makes its conclusion probable. A fallacy is a common pattern of bad reasoning.

read.title: Good form and true premises
text: Philosophers try to answer basic questions about reality, knowledge, and value by giving reasons that others can check. The unit of that checking is the argument: a set of premises offered in support of a conclusion.

Logic separates two questions about any argument. First, do the premises support the conclusion? Second, are the premises true? A deductive argument is valid when its form makes it impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Validity says nothing about whether the premises are in fact true. 'If the moon is cheese, mice live there; the moon is cheese; so mice live there' is valid but unsound. An argument is sound only when it is valid and every premise is true, so a sound argument always has a true conclusion.

Inductive arguments work differently. They reason from observed cases to a probable conclusion, as a doctor does when a treatment has worked in thousands of trials. A strong inductive argument can still have a false conclusion, because new evidence may surprise us. Learning to tell form from content, and certainty from probability, is the first skill a philosophy student needs.

q.q: Why is the moon-and-mice argument valid but unsound?
o: Its form is correct, but a premise is false
Its premises are true, but its form is wrong
It is inductive rather than deductive

q.q: What must be true of a sound argument's conclusion?
o: It may be false if new evidence appears

q.q: According to the reading, how can a strong inductive argument fail?

It can never fail if its premises are true
